items.title: Drift later, an hour a night
items.detail:
LA to Xi'an looks like +15 hours. Your body will take the short way round, which is NINE HOURS BACKWARD — later, not earlier. That is the easy direction, it is the one a westbound Pacific flight already pushes you in, and it means the instruction for this whole week is simply: go to bed later.

Bedtime 23:00, then 00:00, then 01:00, then 02:00, waking as late as the Trybal schedule lets you. Keep the lights on in the evening. Don't set an early alarm you don't need.

On a group trip you will bank two or three of those nine hours, not all of them, and that is fine. Three hours is the difference between boarding at 23:50 wrecked and boarding at 23:50 genuinely awake — which is what the flight plan below depends on.

items.title: Do not catch up on sleep before the flight
items.detail:
The instinct before a long haul is an early night. Resist it.

You want to board tired enough to sleep on demand seven hours in, and NOT so wrecked that you fall asleep the moment you sit down — because the first seven hours of this flight are a Xi'an afternoon and evening, and sleeping through them is precisely what sets the jet lag you are trying to avoid.

items.title: Set your watch to Xi'an time
items.detail:
The single habit that does most of the work, and it costs nothing. From the moment you board, the only clock that exists is Xi'an's. Phone, watch, everything.

KE012 leaves LAX at 23:50 on Saturday the 27th. In Xi'an it is already 14:50 on MONDAY the 28th — you are boarding in the middle of a Xi'an afternoon, and the date line eats Sunday. Think in the new clock and the rest of this page reads as common sense rather than arithmetic.

items.title: Stay awake
items.detail:
Xi'an afternoon and evening. Eat the first meal, watch things, walk the aisle, talk to someone. Keep the window shade up and your reading light on.

This is the hardest instruction on the page and the one that pays for everything else. It is also why the California drift matters: if you have pushed bedtime to 02:00, then 23:50 is early evening to you and staying up is merely boring rather than brutal.

items.title: Sleep
items.detail:
Now it is a Xi'an night, so sleep like it is one. The eye mask and earplugs are already on your packing list and flagged can't-forget — this is the leg they exist for.

If you are using melatonin, this is the moment: 0.5–1 mg, not the 5 or 10 mg most shops sell. Bigger doses are more sedating without being more effective.

items.title: A dim four and a half hours, and no coffee
items.detail:
The clock in the terminal says early morning. Your target clock says the small hours of the night. Believe the target clock.

Find a quiet corner rather than a bright cafe, keep sunglasses on under the terminal lighting if it helps, doze if you can. Above all SKIP THE COFFEE — caffeine here buys you a good layover and costs you the evening you actually need.

items.title: Land. Do not nap. This is the day it is won or lost.
items.detail:
You land late morning on maybe five hours of sleep, and everything in you will want a hotel bed at 13:00. Don't. A nap here is the single thing most likely to leave you broken for three days.

This is exactly why the city wall bike ride sits on the itinerary for this afternoon: outdoor daylight and gentle movement is what actually resets a body clock, and it asks nothing of you but pedalling. Afternoon light in Xi'an lands in the delaying half of your cycle, which is the direction you want — so the more of this afternoon you spend outside, the better tomorrow is.

Drop the bags, get out, and keep moving until dinner.

items.title: Dinner at a local hour, bed by 22:30
items.detail:
Muslim Quarter after dark is already the plan and it is the right one — a real meal at a real local dinner time is itself a strong time cue.

Then stop. Lights down from 21:30, phone out of your hands, bed at 22:00–22:30. Melatonin 0.5–1 mg at 21:30 if you are using it. You will sleep; the flight will have seen to that.

items.title: An early start, against the grain
items.detail:
The Terracotta Warriors need a 07:00 start and it has to be today, so this is the one morning where the jet lag plan and the itinerary pull in opposite directions. Your body will think it is the middle of the night.

Take it anyway — one rough morning beats losing the Warriors to Golden Week tomorrow. Sunglasses on the metro out if the platform lighting feels savage, then get the daylight properly once you are above ground. It is two changes and nearly two hours each way, which is a lot of sitting: walk the three pits rather than dozing on a bench, and do not nap when you get back.

items.title: Caffeine before local noon only
items.detail:
Use it deliberately in the local morning — it is genuinely useful for getting through day one — and then stop at noon.

Caffeine has a five to six hour half-life, so a 16:00 coffee still has a quarter of its dose aboard at bedtime. On the days you are trying to fall asleep at a local hour on an unshifted body, that quarter is enough to cost you the night.

items.when: The whole of Xi'an and Tibet
items.title: No alcohol until Shanghai
items.detail:
It will put you under quickly and then fragment the second half of the night, which is the half that does the consolidating. On a body already fighting a nine-hour move that is a bad trade.

From 2 October it stops being a preference anyway: at altitude alcohol is genuinely a bad idea, and the tour notes already say so. Save it for the Bund.

items.title: Be fixed before the train
items.detail:
This is the part that makes the plan urgent rather than nice-to-have, and it is the reason to take days one and two seriously.

You board the Z165 on 2 October and wake at 3,650 m in Lhasa on the 3rd. Sleep at altitude is disrupted for almost everyone — periodic breathing, repeated waking, and a general sense of never quite going under — and you CANNOT MEDICATE THROUGH IT: no sleeping pills and no alcohol at altitude, which the tour notes already flag.

So anything still broken on 1 October stays broken for a week, on top of whatever the altitude does. You have three nights in Xi'an to land this, and three nights is enough if the first two go as above.

items.title: Use it for sleep onset, not as the mechanism
items.detail:
It is on your packing list and you have it. Take 0.5–1 mg about an hour before target bedtime.

Worth being straight about the evidence, though: melatonin's phase-shifting effect is cleanest for eastward travel, and for a delay this large the timing that would actually shift your clock is awkward and not worth chasing. So treat it as something that helps you fall asleep at a local hour, and let LIGHT AND TIMING do the real work — they are the levers that matter here.

items.title: The easy direction, and no plan needed
items.detail:
Included for completeness rather than because it needs managing. Shanghai to LA is westward and you land at 15:24 on the same calendar day you left; DL899 then runs overnight into Atlanta at 06:07 on the 16th, and Atlanta is only three hours off LA.

Get outside into morning light on the 16th, stay up until a normal Atlanta evening, and it usually clears in two or three days on its own. The hard direction was the one you already did.
